title: PocketBase: A Backend in One File
subtitle: Collections, rules, auth, realtime, files, hooks and production, with Python labs that rebuild the ideas
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: Learn PocketBase, the open source Go backend with an embedded SQLite database. You will design collections and fields, use the records API and the JavaScript SDK, write API rules and filters, sign users in with passwords, OAuth2 and one-time codes, expand relations, subscribe to realtime events, handle files, extend the server with JavaScript hooks and Go, manage migrations, and run it in production with backups and rate limits. Each chapter has an ELI5 block and Python labs.

chapters.title: What PocketBase is

maps.title: PocketBase
links: Executable | serves | REST and realtime API

summary: PocketBase is an open source backend in a single file. It is written in Go and uses an embedded SQLite database.
One program gives you a database, a REST style API, realtime updates, user accounts, file storage and an admin dashboard. You start it with serve.
It is still before version 1.0, so details can change between releases.

glossary.def: The server side of an app: data, accounts, rules.
A database that runs inside your program instead of a separate server.
A small database stored in one file.
The admin web page, served at /_/.
An admin account that bypasses all access rules.
The folder where PocketBase keeps its database and uploaded files.

keyPoints: PocketBase is open source, written in Go and MIT licensed.
It bundles SQLite, a REST style API, realtime subscriptions, auth, files and a dashboard.
Run it with ./pocketbase serve; the default address is 127.0.0.1:8090.
The dashboard is at /_/ and the API is under /api/.
Folders next to the program: pb_data, pb_public, pb_hooks and pb_migrations.
It is pre-1.0, so read the release notes before upgrading.

items: ELI5. PocketBase is a lunchbox that holds a whole kitchen: a notebook for your data, a door guard, a mailbox for files and a doorbell. You carry one box and everything is inside.

Most apps need the same few things from a backend: somewhere to store data, a way to sign users in, rules about who can see what, a way to upload files, and a way to push changes to open screens. Normally that is a database server, an auth service, a file store and glue code.

PocketBase puts all of it in one downloadable program. You download a file, unzip it, and run it. It creates a SQLite database on disk, opens a web server, and gives you a dashboard in the browser where you design your data.

lesson.code:
./pocketbase serve
# API:       http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/
# Dashboard: http://127.0.0.1:8090/_/
./pocketbase superuser create admin@example.com 'a-long-password'

items: Next to the program PocketBase uses a few folders. The pb_data folder holds the SQLite database and uploaded files, so it is the one that matters for backups. The pb_hooks folder holds JavaScript files that extend the server. The pb_migrations folder holds schema changes as code.
Files in pb_public are served as a static website.

You can also use PocketBase as a Go library and build your own program around it. The prebuilt program already includes a JavaScript engine for hooks. Both routes give the same core: collections, rules, auth, realtime and files.

Be aware of the version. PocketBase is still below 1.0 and its authors say backward compatibility is not guaranteed before then. Version 0.23 made large changes, for example admins became superusers. Always read the release notes, and the program can update itself with ./pocketbase update.

quiz.q: Which database does PocketBase embed?
quiz.explain: It is one file on disk.

quiz.q: Where is the admin dashboard by default?
Which folder should you back up?

practice.intro: Match each folder with what it holds.

practice.title: Route kind
practice.intro: Write route_kind(path): return 'dashboard' if the path is /_ or starts with /_/, 'api' if it starts with /api/, otherwise 'static'.

practice.title: Serve flags
practice.intro: Write parse_serve(args): args is a list like ['serve', '--http=0.0.0.0:8080', '--dir=./mydata']. Return [http, dir], using the defaults '127.0.0.1:8090' and 'pb_data' when a flag is missing.

chapters.title: Collections and fields

maps.title: Collections
links: View | is | A read-only SQL query

summary: A collection is a table of records, and each record has fields. There are three types of collection: base for ordinary data, auth for accounts that can sign in, and view for a read-only result of a SQL query.
Every record has an id, created and updated. Fields have types such as text, number, bool, email, url, date, select, file, relation, json and password.
The lab checks records against a field list.

glossary.def: A named set of records, backed by a SQLite table.
One row in a collection.
The default type for general data.
A base collection with sign-in features.
A read-only collection defined by a SQL query.
A field that points to a record in another collection.

keyPoints: Collections are backed by plain SQLite tables.
Base, auth and view are the three collection types.
Every record has id, created and updated.
The default id is a 15 character string of lowercase letters and digits.
Auth collections add email, password, verified and token fields.
View collections never get create, update or delete, and send no realtime events.

items: ELI5. A collection is a labelled tray of index cards. Each card is a record, each line on a card is a field, and the tray says what kind of cards go in it.

Think of a collection as a spreadsheet tab. The columns are fields and the rows are records. Under the hood PocketBase creates a real SQLite table for each collection, so everything you know about SQL indexes and constraints still applies.
The base type is the default. Use it for posts, products, orders and anything else. Each record automatically has an id, which is a 15 character random string, plus created and updated times.

The auth type extends base with what a sign-in needs: an email, a password, a verified flag and a token key. Your own users usually live in an auth collection called users, which exists by default. Superusers live in a special system collection called _superusers.

The view type is different. You give it a SQL query, for example a join that counts comments per post, and it behaves like a read-only collection. You can list and view it, and apply rules, but you cannot create, update or delete, and it sends no realtime events.

Fields have types: text, editor for rich text, number, bool, email, url, date, select, file, relation, json, password and geoPoint, among others. Each type has its own options, such as required, a maximum length, or the allowed values of a select.
Add indexes on the fields you filter and sort by, in the same way you would in any SQL database.

quiz.q: How many collection types are there?
Which collection type is read-only?
What does a relation field store?
options: The id of a record in another collection

cards.q: What does an auth collection add?
Which type has a SQL query?

practice.title: Types
practice.text: The three collection types are {{base}}, {{auth}} and {{view}}.

practice.title: Valid names
practice.intro: Write valid_name(name): a collection name is valid when it is not empty and uses only letters, digits and underscores.

practice.title: Valid ids
practice.intro: Write valid_id(s): true when s is exactly 15 characters, each a lowercase letter a to z or a digit.

practice.title: Validate a record
practice.intro: Write validate(fields, record): fields is a list of [name, type, required] with type 'text', 'number' or 'bool'. record is a dict. Return the sorted list of error strings: 'name: required' when a required field is missing or empty, or 'name: wrong type' when present but not the right kind (a bool is not a number).

chapters.title: The records API

maps.title: Records API
links: List | returns | A page of records

summary: Every collection gets a REST style API automatically. You list, view, create, update and delete records under /api/collections/NAME/records.
A list call returns a page: page, perPage, totalItems, totalPages and items. You can pass sort, filter, expand and fields to shape the result.
The labs compute page counts and parse sort strings.

glossary.def: Returning a long list in pages.
How many records come back in one page.
The order of results, such as -created for newest first.
An expression that keeps only matching records.
A query option that loads related records inside the response.
A query option that returns only some fields.

keyPoints: List is GET /api/collections/NAME/records; view adds /ID.
Create is POST, update is PATCH, delete is DELETE.
A page response has page, perPage, totalItems, totalPages and items.
sort=-created,title sorts newest first, then by title.
filter takes an expression like title ~ 'abc' && created > '2022-01-01'.
Which records you may touch depends on the collection's API rules.

items: ELI5. The API is a counter with five windows: list, look, add, change and remove. You ask politely through a window and get back a page of cards.
When you add a collection, PocketBase already exposes its API. There is nothing to write. The dashboard even has an API preview tab that shows the exact calls for your collection.

A list call returns an object with the page number, the page size, the total count, the number of pages, and the items. Use page and perPage to walk through the list. Sort is a comma separated list of field names, and a minus sign means descending.

The filter option takes a filter expression. The syntax is the same one used in API rules, which you will meet in chapter 5. The expand option asks PocketBase to load related records so that you do not need a second request. The fields option trims the response to the fields you name.

Create and update accept JSON, or multipart form data when files are included. Update is a partial change: only the fields you send are modified. Delete returns an empty success response. Whether any of these calls is allowed depends on the rule for that action.
You will use these calls through the SDK in the next chapter, but they are plain HTTP, so any language can call them, including curl.

quiz.q: Which verb updates a record?
What does sort=-created do?
What does expand do?
options: Loads related records in the response

practice.intro: Match each call with what it does.

practice.title: Total pages
practice.intro: Write total_pages(total, per): the number of pages needed for total items at per items per page. Zero items still give 0 pages.
practice.solution:
def total_pages(total, per):
    return (total + per - 1) // per

practice.title: One page
practice.intro: Write page_of(items, page, per): the items on the given 1-based page. Return an empty list past the end.

practice.title: Parse sort
practice.intro: Write parse_sort(s): turn 'a,-b' into [['a', 'asc'], ['b', 'desc']]. Ignore empty parts.

chapters.title: The JavaScript SDK

maps.title: SDK
links: SDK | works in | Browser and Node

summary: The official JavaScript SDK works in browsers, Node.js and React Native. You create a client with new PocketBase(url) and then work through pb.collection(name).
The common calls are getList, getFullList, getOne, getFirstListItem, create, update and delete.
Never paste user input into a filter string. Use pb.filter with placeholders so values are escaped.

glossary.def: A library that wraps the HTTP API.
Fetches one page of records.
Fetches every record by requesting pages in a loop.
Fetches the first record matching a filter.
Where the SDK keeps the sign-in token and record.
A named slot like {:name} that is filled with an escaped value.

keyPoints: Install with npm install pocketbase, or import it as an ES module in a browser.
pb.collection('posts').getList(1, 20, { filter, sort, expand }) returns one page.
getFullList loops through pages for you, so use it only for small collections.
getFirstListItem fetches one record and errors if none matches.
pb.filter('title = {:t}', { t }) escapes and binds values.
The authStore saves the token and updates after sign-in.

items: ELI5. The SDK is a friendly helper who speaks the counter's language for you. It also washes your words, so a sneaky quote mark cannot trick the counter.
The client keeps one connection setting, the address of the server. Every call goes through pb.collection with the collection name. Methods return promises, so you use await.

The getList call returns a page object with items and counts. The getFullList call fetches every record by requesting pages in a loop. That is convenient but slow for a large collection, so prefer getList with a real filter.
The getFirstListItem call is handy when you expect exactly one match, for example a record found by a unique slug.

Filters need care. If you build a filter by joining a string with user input, a quote in the input can change the meaning of the filter, in the same way SQL injection does. The pb.filter helper takes a template with placeholders like {:q} and a values object, and it escapes each value.

The SDK also keeps the signed-in user in pb.authStore, which holds the token and the record and can be saved in local storage. You will use it in the next chapters. In a browser, the SDK cancels an older request when you send a new identical one, which you can turn off with autoCancellation.

quiz.q: Why use pb.filter?
Which call fetches every record?
Where is the sign-in token kept?

practice.title: SDK
practice.text: You create the client with new {{PocketBase}}(url) and call pb.{{collection}}('posts').getList(1, 20).

practice.title: Bind values
practice.intro: Write pb_filter(tpl, params): replace each {:name} in tpl with the value from params. Strings become single-quoted with any single quote escaped as \' ; booleans become true or false; null (None) becomes null; numbers are written as they are. Leave unknown placeholders unchanged.
practice.hint: Scan for {: and read up to }.

practice.title: Requests for a full list
practice.intro: Write requests_needed(total, batch): how many requests getFullList makes for total records with the given batch size. It always makes at least one.
practice.hint: Round up, but never below one.

chapters.title: API rules: who can do what
summary: API rules are access control and a record filter at once. Each collection has five: listRule, viewRule, createRule, updateRule and deleteRule. Auth collections also have a manage rule.
A rule can be null, which locks the action to superusers, an empty string, which lets anyone in, or an expression that must be true. Superusers always bypass rules.
The labs check rule outcomes and run a small rule evaluator.

glossary.def: A filter expression that decides who may do an action.
A null rule: only superusers may act.
An empty string: anyone may act.
The signed-in record making the request.
The data submitted with the request.
A suffix such as :isset, :changed, :length or :each.

keyPoints: null means locked, an empty string means open, and an expression means conditional.
A failed list rule returns an empty list with status 200; a failed create rule returns 400.
A failed view, update or delete rule returns 404; a locked rule for a non-superuser returns 403.
@request.auth.id != "" means a signed-in user.
@request.body.role:isset = false blocks sending a role field.
Rules also act as filters: a list rule of status = 'active' returns only active records.

items: ELI5. A rule is a bouncer with a short question. Locked means nobody but the owner of the building, empty means everybody, and a question means only people who answer it right.
Rules are the heart of PocketBase security. By default every rule is null, which means locked: only superusers can use the API. You open actions one at a time, as narrowly as you can.

A rule is a filter expression. It is evaluated for the request. For list it works as a filter on the records. For view, update and delete it decides whether the record is visible. For create it decides whether the data may be added. Superusers skip all of it.

The failure codes tell clients what happened. An unmet list rule returns an empty list with status 200, because to the list the records are simply not there. An unmet create rule returns 400. An unmet view, update or delete rule returns 404, as if the record did not exist.
A locked rule returns 403 to anyone who is not a superuser.

Inside a rule you can use the fields of the record, including fields of related records such as author.name. You can read the request with @request.auth for the signed-in user, @request.body for submitted data, @request.query for query parameters, @request.headers and @request.method.
The @collection prefix lets a rule look at another collection that shares a value.

Modifiers add checks. The :isset modifier asks whether the client sent a field. The :changed modifier asks whether a submitted value differs from the stored one. The :length modifier counts items in a multiple field, and :each applies a condition to every item.
Operators include =, !=, comparisons, ~ for like, and a question mark variant such as ?= that means any item matches. Macros such as @now and @todayStart are in UTC.

quiz.explain: As if it were not there.

quiz.q: What does an empty string rule mean?

practice.title: Rule values
practice.intro: Match each rule value with its meaning.

practice.title: Rule value
practice.intro: Write rule_kind(rule, is_superuser): rule is null (None), an empty string, or an expression. Return 'allow' for superusers and for an empty rule, 'locked' for null, and 'check' for an expression.

practice.title: Failure status
practice.intro: Write fail_status(action, locked): the HTTP status when the rule fails. A locked rule gives 403 for any action. Otherwise list gives 200, create gives 400, and view, update and delete give 404.

practice.title: A tiny rule evaluator
practice.intro: Write check(rule, record, auth): evaluate a rule made of clauses joined by && and || (|| binds weaker, no parentheses). Each clause is 'left op right' with spaces around op, where op is one of = != > >= < <= ~ !~. Operands: a quoted string, true, false, a number, @request.auth.FIELD (from auth, empty string if missing) or a field of record (empty string if missing). The ~ operator is a case-insensitive contains, or starts-with / ends-with when the right side ends / starts with %.

chapters.title: Authentication

maps.title: Auth
links: OAuth2 | signs in | With Google or GitHub

summary: Any auth collection can sign users in. The classic way is a password: the server checks it and returns a signed token, a JWT, plus the record.
The client sends the token in the Authorization header on later requests. The SDK keeps it in the authStore.
PocketBase also supports OAuth2 providers, one-time passwords by email, and multi-factor authentication. Superusers sign in the same way, but cannot use OAuth2.

glossary.def: A signed token with three parts: header, payload and signature.
The SDK's storage for the token and the signed-in record.
Signing in through another service like Google or GitHub.
A one-time password sent by email.
Multi-factor authentication: two methods in a row.
Confirming that a user owns their email address.

keyPoints: pb.collection('users').authWithPassword(email, password) returns the token and record.
A JWT has header, payload and signature, joined by dots; the payload carries the id and the expiry.
The token goes in the Authorization header.
OAuth2 uses the redirect address /api/oauth2-redirect; _superusers do not support OAuth2.
requestOTP returns an otpId, even if the email is unknown, so attackers cannot probe for accounts.
Record creation does not sign the user in; you sign in after creating.

items: ELI5. A token is a stamped wristband you get after proving who you are. You show the wristband each time, and it stops working after a while.

Sign-in works on auth collections. A user record has an email and a password, and the server never stores the password itself, only a hash. You create the account with a normal create call. Creating does not sign anyone in.

The token is a JSON Web Token. It is three parts joined by dots: a header, a payload and a signature. The payload holds claims such as the record id, the collection and the expiry time. The signature proves that the server issued it.
The client sends it in the Authorization header, and the SDK does that for you.

OAuth2 lets users sign in with Google, GitHub and many other providers. You enable a provider in the collection settings with its client id and secret, and use the redirect address on your own server, ending in /api/oauth2-redirect.
In the browser, authWithOAuth2 opens a popup and finishes the flow. Superusers are the exception: OAuth2 is not supported for the _superusers collection.

A one-time password sends a short code to the user's email. You call requestOTP, which returns an otpId, and then authWithOTP with that id and the code. The otpId is returned even when no such user exists, so nobody can use it to find out which emails are registered.
For sensitive apps, combine OTP with another method using multi-factor authentication.

Verification is separate: it confirms that a user controls an email address, by sending a link. A rule can then require @request.auth.verified = true. Next to sign-in there are helpers for password reset and for changing an email address.

quiz.q: What does a JWT payload usually carry?
options: The record id and the expiry

quiz.q: Does creating a user sign them in?
Which collection does not support OAuth2?

practice.title: Sign in
practice.text: Use pb.collection('users').{{authWithPassword}}(email, password), and the token is kept in pb.{{authStore}}.

practice.title: Token status
practice.intro: Write token_status(token, now): the token has three parts joined by dots, and the middle part is base64url JSON with an integer exp (expiry seconds). Return 'malformed' if it does not have three parts, cannot be decoded, or has no integer exp; 'expired' if now is at or after exp; otherwise 'valid'. (The signature is not checked here, only a server can do that.)
practice.hint: Decode the middle part by hand.

practice.title: OTP check
practice.intro: Write otp_check(stored, entered, issued, now, ttl): return 'expired' when now - issued is at least ttl seconds, otherwise 'ok' if the codes are equal, otherwise 'wrong'.

chapters.title: Relations, expand and view collections
summary: A relation field stores the id of a record in another collection, or several ids for a multiple relation. Rules can follow relations too, for example author.verified = true.
The expand option loads the related records in the same response, under record.expand. Nested paths like author.team work too, and a back-relation can be expanded in the other direction.
The labs join records and find back-relations.

glossary.def: A field holding the id or ids of other records.
Loading related records into record.expand.
The records in another collection that point at this one.
Deleting dependent records when the parent is deleted.
A relation field that holds a list of ids.
Combining rows of two tables by a shared value.

keyPoints: A relation stores ids, so a plain read shows only an id like author: 'abc123'.
expand: 'author' adds record.expand.author with the full record.
Nested paths use dots: expand: 'author.team'.
Related records you may not view are left out of expand, because their view rule applies.
A back-relation expand uses the form COLLECTION_via_FIELD.
cascadeDelete true removes dependent records; false blocks deleting the parent.

items: ELI5. A relation is a sticky note on one card saying see card number 12 in the other tray. Expanding is walking over and bringing card 12 back with you.

A relation is a pointer. In a posts collection you add an author field of type relation that points to users. The stored value is the user's id. The API returns that id by default, because returning a whole user inside every post would be wasteful.

When you do want the user, ask for it with expand. The SDK puts the loaded record in record.expand.author, never directly on the record. You can expand several fields at once, separated by commas, and go deeper with dots, such as author.team.
Access rules still apply to expanded records. If you may not view the author record, it simply does not appear in expand. This keeps a relation from leaking data that the target's own rules protect.

What happens when you delete a record that others point at? A relation field has a cascadeDelete option. When it is true, deleting the parent removes the dependent records. When it is false, the parent cannot be deleted until the dependents are gone or changed.
Choose false for important data like orders.

When you need aggregates, such as a post and its comment count, create a view collection. It is a SQL query, so joins and GROUP BY are available. It is read-only and sends no realtime events, but it can have list and view rules like any other collection.

practice.intro: Write expand_paths(s): split an expand string like 'author,comments.user' into a list of paths, each a list of names: [['author'], ['comments', 'user']]. Ignore empty parts.

practice.intro: Write expand(posts, users): posts is a list of [post_id, author_id], users is a list of [user_id, name]. Return a list of [post_id, name] with None for a missing author.

chapters.title: Realtime subscriptions

maps.title: Realtime
links: Topic | is | Collection and star or id

summary: Realtime uses Server-Sent Events, a one-way stream from server to browser. The client opens a connection, the server answers with a client id, and then the client says what it wants to follow.
You subscribe to a whole collection with the star topic or to one record by id. Each event says whether a record was created, updated or deleted.
The same rules apply: you only receive events for records you may view.

glossary.def: Server-Sent Events: a long-lived HTTP response that streams messages to the client.
A request to receive events for a topic.
What you follow: a collection (star) or one record id.
A message with an action and the changed record.
The first event, carrying the client id.
A topic you publish yourself from server code.

keyPoints: The realtime API is SSE with two steps: connect, then submit subscriptions.
SSE events are sent for create, update and delete.
pb.collection('posts').subscribe('*', cb) follows the collection; subscribe(id, cb) follows one record.
Events respect the list and view rules, and a subscribe can take filter and fields options.
View collections send no realtime events.
The SDK reconnects by itself and resubscribes.

items: ELI5. Realtime is a doorbell for changes. You tell the house what you care about, and it rings your phone the moment a card is added, changed or thrown away.

Normal HTTP is request and answer. Realtime flips it: the screen keeps one connection open and the server pushes news when it has some. PocketBase uses Server-Sent Events for this, which is plain HTTP, one direction, and works through ordinary proxies.

The flow has two steps. First the client opens the stream and the server immediately sends an event called PB_CONNECT with a client id. Second, the client posts its list of topics along with that id. A topic is a collection followed by a star, or a collection followed by a record id.

Rules matter here as well. For each event the server checks whether this client would be allowed to view the record, using the collection's rules. A client that may not see a record never learns that it changed. The filter option narrows a subscription further, and fields trims what is sent.
On the client you typically keep a list in memory. On create you add the record, on update you replace it by id, and on delete you remove it. That gives you a live list with very little code.

You can also publish your own topics from JavaScript or Go on the server, and the browser subscribes with pb.realtime.subscribe. Remember that every open client is a connection: for large audiences raise the open file limit of the host, as the production chapter explains.

quiz.q: What does realtime use?
What does subscribe('*') follow?
What do the rules decide?

cards.a: The first event with a client id.

practice.title: Realtime
practice.intro: Match each item with its role.

practice.title: Who gets the event
practice.intro: Write dispatch(subs, event): subs is a list of [client, topic] where topic is 'collection/*' or 'collection/id'. event is [collection, record_id]. Return the sorted list of distinct clients subscribed to either the collection star topic or that record.
practice.hint: Compare each topic with both wanted topics.

practice.title: Keep a live list
practice.intro: Write apply_event(items, event): items is a list of [id, title]. event is [action, id, title]. Create appends, update replaces the title of the item with that id, delete removes it. Return the new list.

chapters.title: Files and storage
summary: A file field stores uploads in the record. You send them as multipart form data, and PocketBase saves them on disk under pb_data, or in an S3 compatible store if you configure one.
Each file is served at /api/files/COLLECTION/RECORD/FILENAME. For images you can ask for a thumbnail with the thumb query parameter.
A protected file needs a short-lived file token and obeys the view rule.

glossary.def: A field that holds one or more uploaded file names.
An HTTP body format that can carry files.
A resized copy of an image, requested as WxH.
A file that can only be fetched with a token and a passing rule.
Storing uploads in an object store instead of on local disk.
The kind of a file, such as image/png.

keyPoints: File fields set maxSelect, maxSize and allowed MIME types.
The record keeps the file name; the file lives under pb_data/storage/COLLECTION_ID/RECORD_ID/.
PocketBase adds a random suffix to uploaded names so they do not collide.
The URL is /api/files/COLLECTION/RECORD_ID/FILENAME, and ?thumb=100x100 returns a thumbnail.
Thumb sizes must be listed in the field options.
Protected files are fetched with ?token= from a file token request.

items: ELI5. A file field is a coat check. You hand in a coat, you get a ticket with a new name, and the ticket is only good for your own coat.

A file field is an ordinary field in your collection. Set whether it holds one file or several, the maximum size, and which MIME types are allowed. In the browser you send a FormData object, or a plain object with File values in the SDK, which turns it into a multipart request.

On disk the file goes under the pb_data folder in a path made of the collection id and the record id. PocketBase adds a short random suffix to the name, so two people who upload photo.png do not overwrite each other. The record stores the new name.
The public address is made of /api/files, the collection, the record id and the filename. For images you can add thumb with a size like 100x100. A size with a zero keeps the proportions, like 0x300.

An optional letter after the size chooses how to crop: t for the top, b for the bottom, f to fit inside. The sizes must be allowed in the field settings, so nobody can ask for a thousand different thumbnails.

Files are public by default if you know the address. If a field is set as protected, the file can only be fetched with a short-lived token that you request while signed in. The token is checked against the record's view rule, and a rule can see the case with @request.context = "protectedFile".

If you run several servers or want cheap storage, switch to an S3 compatible store in the settings. Backups can go to S3 too. Remember that local files live in pb_data, so back them up with the database.

practice.title: Files
practice.text: A file is served at /api/{{files}}/COLLECTION/RECORD/FILENAME and a thumbnail is requested with ?{{thumb}}=100x100.

practice.title: File address
practice.intro: Write file_url(base, collection, record_id, filename, thumb): return base (without a trailing slash) + '/api/files/' + collection + '/' + record_id + '/' + filename, and add '?thumb=' + thumb when thumb is not None.

practice.title: Parse a thumb size
practice.intro: Write parse_thumb(spec): a size is WxH with an optional last letter t, b or f. Return [width, height, mode] where mode is 'center' by default, or 't', 'b', 'f' for the letter, or 'resize' when either number is 0. Return an empty list when the spec is invalid (not two numbers, or both zero).

practice.title: Upload check
practice.intro: Write upload_errors(mime, size, allowed, max_size): return a sorted list of problems: 'too large' when size is over max_size, and 'type not allowed' when allowed is not empty and mime is not in it.

chapters.title: Extending with JavaScript
summary: The prebuilt PocketBase runs JavaScript files that end in .pb.js from the pb_hooks folder. With them you add routes, react to events, and schedule jobs, without compiling anything.
An event hook is a function that receives an event e. Code before e.next runs before the action, code after it runs after. Not calling e.next, or throwing, stops the chain.
The engine is goja, a JavaScript interpreter written in Go, so it supports ES5 and a good part of newer syntax, but no ES modules.

glossary.def: A function that runs when something happens.
The object a hook receives, with the app and the record or request.
Passes control to the next handler and then to the action itself.
Registers a custom HTTP route.
Registers a job on a cron schedule.
The JavaScript engine inside PocketBase.

keyPoints: Put hooks in pb_hooks/*.pb.js next to the executable.
routerAdd('GET', '/hello/{name}', (e) => e.json(200, {...})) adds a route.
onRecordCreate runs before the insert; onRecordAfterCreateSuccess runs after it commits.
A hook must call e.next() to continue; throwing an error stops the chain.
You can add collection names after the handler to run it only for those collections.
cronAdd('name', '*/30 * * * *', fn) runs a job on a five field cron schedule.

items: ELI5. A hook is a little helper standing at a door who can tidy a thing before it goes in, or say stop. If the helper does not wave it on, it does not go through.

Any file in the pb_hooks folder that ends in .pb.js is loaded when the server starts. Inside it you use global functions like routerAdd, onRecordCreate and cronAdd, and the global $app for the running application. The __hooks variable gives the absolute path to the folder.

Routes give you endpoints that the automatic API does not have, for example a call that charges a card. A route handler receives an event e and answers with e.json, e.string and similar helpers. You can add middleware such as a check that the caller is signed in.

Event hooks wrap things that PocketBase does. Think of onRecordCreate as a function around the insert. Code you put before e.next runs first. Calling e.next lets the next handler and then the real insert run. Code after e.next runs after the insert returns.
If you throw, or never call e.next, the chain stops and the insert does not happen.
There are also hooks for after success and after error, for requests, for authentication, for mail, and for the server starting. Pass collection names after the handler to limit it.
For editor help, add a reference line to pb_data/types.d.ts at the top of your file, and the editor will know every function.

The hook engine is for small amounts of logic. Each file is loaded in a sandbox, and handlers do not share mutable state, so keep shared data in the database. If your logic grows, you can move to the Go framework in the next chapter.

quiz.q: Where do hook files go?
What happens if a hook never calls e.next()?
Which engine runs the hooks?

practice.title: Hooks
practice.intro: Match each function with its job.

practice.title: Hook chain
practice.intro: Write run_chain(handlers): handlers is a list of booleans, true when that handler calls e.next(). Handler i logs 'i:before' first. If it calls next, the next handler runs (or, after the last handler, the action logs 'INSERT'), and then it logs 'i:after'. A handler that does not call next logs nothing more. Return the log list.

practice.title: Cron match
practice.intro: Write cron_match(expr, minute, hour, dom, month, dow): true when the five field cron expression matches. Each field may be *, */n, a number, a range a-b, or a comma list of those. Fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week (0 is Sunday). */n counts from the first value of the field (0 for minute, hour and weekday, 1 for day and month).

chapters.title: Go framework, migrations and the CLI

maps.title: Go
links: Superuser | is created | From the CLI

summary: Instead of the prebuilt program you can import PocketBase into your own Go program. You call pocketbase.New, register routes and hooks, and build one static executable.
Schema changes are stored as migration files in pb_migrations, named with a timestamp. When you change collections in the dashboard in development, PocketBase writes a migration for you.
Everyday commands are serve, superuser create, migrate and update.

glossary.def: Using PocketBase as a Go library to build your own backend.
A file that changes the schema in a repeatable way.
Writing migration files automatically when collections change.
The command line: serve, superuser, migrate, update.
An executable with no outside dependencies.
A command to make an admin account.

keyPoints: Create main.go with pocketbase.New() and register routes inside app.OnServe().
Build a static executable with CGO_ENABLED=0 go build, then run ./myapp serve.
Migration files live in pb_migrations and are named TIMESTAMP_description.js (or .go).
Applied migrations are recorded in the database so each runs once.
./pocketbase superuser create EMAIL PASSWORD makes an admin.
./pocketbase update updates the prebuilt executable.

items: ELI5. Migrations are a diary of changes to the trays, with dates. Anyone can replay the diary in order and end up with the same trays.
The prebuilt program is enough for most apps. Choose the Go route when you want to write your server logic in Go, or ship one custom executable. Both routes give the same collections, rules and API.

The Go module path is shown in the Go documentation for your version, so copy the import lines from there. After go mod tidy you can run go run main.go serve, or build a single static executable with CGO_ENABLED=0 go build and copy it to a server.

A migration is a file in pb_migrations that changes the schema, for example to create a collection or add a field. Its name starts with a Unix timestamp so that they run in order, followed by a short description. Each file has an up function and a down function.
PocketBase records which ones have run, so each is applied once.

When you work in the dashboard on your own machine, PocketBase can create these files for you whenever you change a collection. Commit them to git. On the production server the new files run on start, or with the migrate command, so the schema follows the code.

lesson.code:
./pocketbase serve                       # run the server
./pocketbase superuser create a@b.com pw   # create an admin
./pocketbase migrate                       # apply pending migrations
./pocketbase update                        # update the prebuilt binary
./pocketbase --dir=./mydata serve          # use a different data folder

practice.title: CLI
practice.text: Run ./pocketbase {{serve}} to start the server and ./pocketbase {{migrate}} to apply pending migrations.

practice.title: Read a migration name
practice.intro: Write parse_migration(name): a file name like '1700000000_created_posts.js' gives [1700000000, 'created_posts'] (the timestamp as an integer, and the description without the .js or .go ending).

practice.title: Pending migrations
practice.intro: Write pending(files, applied): return the sorted list of file names in files that are not in applied, ordered by their numeric timestamp prefix.
practice.hint: Sort by the number, not the text.

practice.title: Schema diff
practice.intro: Write schema_diff(old, new): old and new are lists of field names. Return [added, removed], each a sorted list: added are in new but not old, removed are in old but not new.

chapters.title: Going to production

maps.title: Production
links: Binary | runs | On a small server

summary: Running PocketBase for real takes a few steps. Put it on a small server with a persistent pb_data folder, serve it over HTTPS, back it up, and turn on rate limiting.
Built-in backups make a ZIP snapshot of pb_data and can run on a cron schedule, keeping the newest few. For a very large pb_data, use a different strategy such as an SQLite backup copy.
The labs rotate backups and simulate a rate limiter.

glossary.def: A web server in front of PocketBase, such as Nginx or Caddy.
A copy of pb_data that you can restore.
How many scheduled backups to keep before removing older ones.
A rule that limits requests per time window.
A secret used to encrypt the settings stored in the database.
The operating system limit on simultaneous connections and files.

keyPoints: Persist the pb_data folder; in Docker mount it as a volume.
serve with a domain name can handle HTTPS with an automatic Let's Encrypt certificate, or put Nginx or Caddy in front.
Backups are ZIP snapshots of pb_data and can be scheduled by cron, with cronMaxKeep controlling how many remain.
Large data folders, about 2 GB or more, need a different backup plan.
The built-in rate limiter takes rules with a label, max requests and duration.
--encryptionEnv=NAME encrypts the settings with a key from an environment variable; never lose that key.

items: ELI5. Production is taking the lunchbox out of your bedroom and putting it in a safe place: a lock on the door, photocopies of the notebook, and a limit on how fast people can knock.

PocketBase is a single process, so production is simple. A small virtual machine is enough for many apps. Scale up with a bigger machine, because SQLite lives on one server, and plan for that from the start.
Start with persistence. The pb_data folder holds the database and the uploaded files. On a server, keep it on a real disk, and in Docker mount a volume on it. Next, serve over HTTPS.
You can start the program with your domain name and let it fetch a certificate, or put Nginx or Caddy in front of it as a reverse proxy.

lesson.code:
# serve a domain over HTTPS with an automatic certificate
./pocketbase serve yourdomain.com

# or listen locally behind a reverse proxy
./pocketbase serve --http=127.0.0.1:8090

# encrypt settings with a key from the environment
export PB_ENCRYPTION_KEY="a-random-32-character-secret-key!"
./pocketbase serve --encryptionEnv=PB_ENCRYPTION_KEY

items: Back up before you need to. The dashboard can create a snapshot, which is a ZIP of pb_data, and can schedule one with a cron expression, such as 0 0 * * *. The setting cronMaxKeep removes old ones. While a snapshot is created the app is briefly read-only.
For a big data folder, a hot copy with the sqlite3 backup command plus rsync is gentler. Test restoring.

Protect the front door. The built-in rate limiter takes rules, each with a label, a maximum number of requests and a duration, and it can apply to a whole path, such as the sign-in route. Use strong passwords for superusers and turn on multi-factor authentication for them.
Configure an SMTP server so that verification and reset emails are sent.

Many open realtime clients are many open connections. If you see too many open files errors, raise the file limit for the process. Setting GOMEMLIMIT gives Go a soft memory limit on a small server. If storage grows, move uploads to S3.

quiz.q: What should be persisted?
What does a backup snapshot contain?
Why raise the open file limit?

practice.title: Production
practice.intro: Match each setting with its purpose.

practice.title: Rotate backups
practice.intro: Write rotate_backups(names, max_keep): names are backup file names that sort oldest first. Return the sorted list of names to delete so that only the newest max_keep remain.

practice.title: Rate limiter
practice.intro: Write rate_limit(times, max_requests, duration): times is the list of request times in seconds, in order. Use fixed windows: window = time // duration. Return a list of booleans, true when the request is allowed (the count in its window, including this one, is at most max_requests).

chapters.title: Designing an app and knowing the limits

maps.title: Design
links: Notes app | uses | Auth and rules
Owner field | links | Record and user
Create rule | forces | Owner is me

summary: A good PocketBase app is mostly collections and rules. Take a notes app: a notes collection with an owner relation to users, and rules that let each person see and change only their own notes.
PocketBase fits small and medium apps, prototypes, internal tools and mobile backends well. It is less suited to apps that need many servers writing at once.
The last labs audit rules and tie the course together.

glossary.def: A relation to users that marks who owns a record.
Giving each action only the access it needs.
Making one server bigger instead of adding more.
SQLite lets one write happen at a time.
Reviewing rules for actions that are too open.
Not yet stable: changes may break things.

keyPoints: Start with all rules locked and open each action as narrowly as possible.
Ownership pattern: author = @request.auth.id for list, view, update and delete.
Create rule: @request.auth.id != "" && @request.body.author = @request.auth.id.
Block ownership changes with @request.body.author:changed = false.
SQLite handles many readers and one writer at a time; scale up one server first.
Before upgrading, read the release notes and test a copy of pb_data.

items: ELI5. Before you build, ask who may look at each card and who may change it. Start with every door locked and open them one at a time.

Let us design a notes app from start to finish. You need two collections. The users collection already exists as an auth collection. Add a notes collection with a title text field, a body editor field and an owner relation field that points to users.

Now the rules. Leave them all locked and open them one by one. Listing and viewing should show only your own notes, so the rule is owner = @request.auth.id. Creating should require sign-in and force the new note to be yours. Updating should let the owner edit but not hand the note to someone else.
Deleting should be owner only.

lesson.code:
// notes collection rules
listRule:   owner = @request.auth.id
viewRule:   owner = @request.auth.id
createRule: @request.auth.id != "" && @request.body.owner = @request.auth.id
updateRule: owner = @request.auth.id && @request.body.owner:changed = false
deleteRule: owner = @request.auth.id

items: Add realtime and the owner's open screens stay in sync with no extra code, because the list rule decides which events each client sees. Add a file field and attachments work, with the same rules.

Know the limits. SQLite allows many readers but a single writer at a time, so an app with very heavy parallel writes will hit a ceiling, and you cannot spread one database over many servers. For most apps a well-sized single server goes a very long way.
If you outgrow it you can still move the data elsewhere.

Also remember the version. PocketBase is pre-1.0, with breaking changes allowed. Pin the version in your deployment, read the release notes, keep migrations in git, and test an upgrade on a copy of pb_data first. With those habits you have a backend that is small, fast to build on, and easy to run.

practice.title: Design
practice.intro: Match each need with the tool.

practice.title: Open write rules
practice.intro: Write open_writes(rules): rules is a dict of action to rule value (None for locked, a string otherwise). Return the sorted list of the write actions create, update and delete whose rule is the empty string (open to anyone).
practice.hint: Look at the write actions only.

practice.title: Ownership rule
practice.intro: Write ownership_rule(field): return the update rule that lets only the owner edit and blocks changing the owner field, exactly: FIELD = @request.auth.id && @request.body.FIELD:changed = false (with FIELD replaced).
practice.solution:
def ownership_rule(field):
    return field + ' = @request.auth.id && @request.body.' + field + ':changed = false'

practice.title: Lock check
practice.intro: Write is_locked(rule, is_superuser): true when a normal user is denied. A null rule (None) denies a normal user; an empty string never denies; any other rule is conditional so return false. Superusers are never denied.
